pr_title: drivers: timer: it8xxx2: fix the timer drift issue
pr_body:
This commit enhances the accuracy of hardware cycle calculation before setting the IT8xxx2 event timer. The next target cycle is calculated by the last, elapsed, and expected timeout ticks. And then, the difference in hardware cycles between the target cycle and the current cycle is set into the event timer. This increased accuracy effectively resolves the clock drift issue.

Tested with:
west build -p always -b it8xxx2_evb tests/kernel/timer/timer_api -T kernel.timer.tickless
west build -p always -b it8xxx2_evb tests/kernel/timer/timer_behavior -T kernel.timer.timer

Fixes #67474 #67833
pr_comments: Tests pass with those changes, checked for #67474

hi @pkunieck,

The it8xxx2 chip needs more time to resume from the low-power mode and the default ```CONFIG_PM``` for it8xxx2_evb is disabled. However, it's enabled in the ```prj_tickless.conf```. We would disable PM for the specific platform(it8xxx2_evb) in ```testcase.yml``` to address this issue.([disable-pm-for-it8xxx2-evb](https://github.com/Chenhongren/zephyr/tree/pr-disable-pm-for-timer-api))

review_comments:
Nitpick: expressing this as a CLAMP() instead of the likely-tagged branch is probably going to generate better code.  Even more so if you can roll the clamp into the ticks computation above.

Just in general the unlikely() construction tends to hurt and not help (both code and readability) if the blocks are tiny one-liners.  Let the branch predictor do its job.

Finally: does a clamp of 1 actually work?  Most timer hardware is based on an equality test in the counter and will drop interrupts if you try to set a deadline too close in the future, and in any case "1" is going to have aliasing bugs where it really lands in the register at a time when it should have been "0".  Some hardware does a proper comparator though, so maybe not necessary.
